strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed attributes addresses a limitation of image-only and text-only retrieval. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets, with additional screening for missing positive matches.

Word4Per provides a practical approach that requires no composed-retrieval training triplets. The lightweight inversion network and frozen encoders in the second stage make the method relatively accessible and straightforward to implement.

The reported improvements are substantial across both backbones. With ViT-L/14, Table 1 reports 45.91% Rank-1 and 55.63% mAP, compared with 35.38% and 44.08% for the text-plus-clothes-changing baseline. Table B also provides useful controlled evidence: identity-aware matching improves Rank-1 over ITC by approximately 3.1–3.4 percentage points.

The framework is generally understandable, and the supplementary experiments examine architecture, prompts, training-data volume, supervision, and ensemble efficiency. Optimizer settings, training schedules, hardware, and approximate training times provide useful reproducibility information.
weaknesses: The main comparison with prior composed-retrieval methods is confounded. Section 5.2 and Table 1 indicate that Pic2Word and SEARLE retain inversion networks trained with original CLIP parameters, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. Word4Per instead trains its inversion network against the adapted encoders on person-domain data. This introduces an encoder–mapper mismatch and unequal adaptation. Matched retraining is needed to establish the claimed methodological advantage; Table B only partially resolves this concern.

Test-set model selection undermines the evaluation protocol. Section 4 designates ITCPR exclusively for testing, but Section 5.3 selects network depth, width, prompt, and token length using benchmark performance. No independent validation protocol or untouched final test set is described. Repeated-run uncertainty is also absent, particularly limiting conclusions about small prompt and fusion improvements.

Methodological originality is limited. The approach combines person-domain CLIP fine-tuning from existing retrieval work, the image-to-pseudo-word mechanism already central to Pic2Word/SEARLE, and established identity-aware matching losses. The benchmark and application are meaningful contributions, but the manuscript needs a sharper account of what new capability or insight goes beyond adapting these components.

Benchmark validation is incomplete. Results are aggregated across the three source datasets without breakdowns by source or clothing-change type. Annotation agreement and the completeness of the encoder-assisted positive-label screening are not quantified. Consequently, the evidence does not establish how reliably the benchmark measures identity-preserving composition across its different settings.

A material implementation ambiguity remains: Table 1 labels the best configuration as L_Vis + L_Text, and the main text describes combined supervision, whereas Appendix C.4 associates these results with fusion of multiple TINets. The paper should distinguish joint optimization of one network from ensembling independently trained networks and specify the exact configuration behind each result.

Ethical documentation is insufficient for a benchmark intended to identify people across images. The manuscript does not explain source-data permissions and redistribution conditions or discuss privacy, surveillance misuse, and potentially unequal identification errors. These are relevant reporting gaps, although the principal reasons for rejection are the uncontrolled comparisons and test-set selection.
